questions.prompt: Pure (intrinsic) silicon is in thermal equilibrium at 300 K. How do the free-electron concentration \(n\) and hole concentration \(p\) compare?
options: \(n > p\), because electrons are lighter and break free more easily
\(n = p = n_i \approx 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)
\(n = p = 5\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), one per atom
questions.explanation:
Every thermally broken bond creates one electron AND one hole, and every recombination removes one of each, so \(n_0 = p_0\) (reader Sec. 3.4.1). Their common value is the intrinsic concentration, \(n_i \approx 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) at 300 K (Eq. 3.27).
The electron's lighter mass affects mobility, not the count. One carrier per atom describes a metal.

questions.prompt: For silicon at 300 K, \(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). What is the equilibrium product \(n\,p\)? Scientific notation is fine.
questions.explanation:
The law of mass action: \(n\,p = n_i^2 = (10^{10})^2 = 10^{20}\ \mathrm{cm^{-6}}\) (reader Eq. 3.28).
This product is fixed by temperature and material alone. It holds in ANY silicon in thermal equilibrium, doped or not, which is what makes it so useful.

questions.prompt: 'Thermal equilibrium' in a semiconductor means which of the following?
options: No bonds break and no carriers recombine
Carriers are still constantly generated and recombining, but the two rates are exactly equal, so the concentrations don't change
All carriers have recombined, so n = p = 0
Generation is faster than recombination, but the extra carriers leave through the contacts
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is a dynamic balance: \(G_{th}(T) = R = k\,n\,p\) (reader Eq. 3.24–3.26). Bonds break and carriers annihilate all the time; on average the rates cancel. Setting them equal is exactly what gives \(np = G_{th}/k = n_i^2\).

questions.prompt: In a piece of silicon at 300 K in thermal equilibrium, the electron concentration is known to be \(n = 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). What is the hole concentration? (\(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\))
questions.explanation:
\[p = \frac{n_i^2}{n} = \frac{10^{20}}{10^{15}} = 10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\]
Raising \(n\) by \(10^5\) above \(n_i\) lowers \(p\) by \(10^5\): with more electrons around, holes recombine faster until the product falls back to \(n_i^2\). Common mistake: assuming \(p\) stays at \(n_i\).

questions.prompt: Using \(n_i \propto e^{-E_g/2kT}\) (ignore the weaker temperature dependence of the prefactor), with \(E_g = 1.12\ \mathrm{eV}\) and \(k = 8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K}\): by what factor does silicon's \(n_i\) grow when it is heated from 300 K to 350 K?
questions.explanation:
\[\frac{n_i(350)}{n_i(300)} = \exp\!\left[\frac{E_g}{2k}\left(\frac{1}{300}-\frac{1}{350}\right)\right]\]
\[\frac{E_g}{2k} = \frac{1.12}{1.7234\times10^{-4}} = 6499\ \mathrm{K}, \quad \frac{1}{300}-\frac{1}{350} = 4.762\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\]
\[\text{factor} = e^{3.095} \approx 22.1\]
A 50 K rise gives about 20 times more carriers. Common mistakes: forgetting the 2 in \(2kT\) (giving about 490) or using \(T\) in °C.
questions.figure_alt: Plot of intrinsic concentration relative to its 300 K value, rising steeply with temperature.

questions.prompt: Away from equilibrium, the recombination rate is modelled as \(R = k\,n\,p\). In a sample where both \(n\) and \(p\) are suddenly doubled, how does \(R\) change (at first)?
options: It becomes 4 times larger
It doubles
It does not change, because the generation rate is fixed
It halves
questions.explanation:
\(R' = k(2n)(2p) = 4\,knp = 4R\). Meanwhile thermal generation \(G_{th}(T)\) stays the same, so \(R > G\) and the excess carriers recombine until \(np\) falls back to \(n_i^2\).
This is the 'chance of meeting' picture: twice as many electrons, each finding twice as many holes.

questions.prompt: At 300 K, rank the intrinsic carrier concentrations of germanium (\(E_g = 0.66\) eV), silicon (1.12 eV) and gallium arsenide (1.42 eV).
options: \(n_{i,GaAs} > n_{i,Si} > n_{i,Ge}\)
They are all equal at the same temperature
\(n_{i,Si} > n_{i,Ge} > n_{i,GaAs}\)
\(n_{i,Ge} > n_{i,Si} > n_{i,GaAs}\)
questions.explanation:
\(n_i \propto e^{-E_g/2kT}\): a SMALLER gap gives exponentially MORE carriers. Each 0.1 eV of gap is a factor of \(e^{0.1/0.052} \approx 7\).
Gotcha: a wider gap does not mean 'more energy available'; it is a taller wall to jump. Equal temperature doesn't mean equal carriers; the gap matters exponentially. (Approximate values: Ge about \(2\times10^{13}\), Si \(10^{10}\), GaAs about \(2\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\).)

questions.prompt: With \(n_i \propto e^{-E_g/2kT}\), \(E_g = 1.12\ \mathrm{eV}\), \(k = 8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K}\): to what temperature must silicon be heated from 300 K to DOUBLE \(n_i\)? Give the answer in kelvin to the nearest 0.5 K.
questions.explanation:
Set \(\exp[\tfrac{E_g}{2k}(\tfrac{1}{300}-\tfrac{1}{T})] = 2\):
\[\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{300} - \frac{\ln 2}{E_g/2k} = 3.3333\times10^{-3} - \frac{0.6931}{6499} = 3.2267\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\]
\[T \approx 309.9\ \mathrm{K}\]
Gotcha: only about 10 K doubles the carrier count. You might expect 'double \(T\)' or a linear rule. This extreme sensitivity is exactly why circuits can't rely on intrinsic carriers.
questions.figure_alt: Plot of the intrinsic concentration ratio versus temperature near 300 K with a dashed line marking a doubling.

questions.prompt: Steady light shines on a piece of pure silicon, generating extra electron–hole pairs. In the steady state under illumination, how does \(np\) compare with \(n_i^2\)?
options: \(np = n_i^2\) always, because the mass-action law is universal
\(np < n_i^2\), because recombination speeds up
\(np > n_i^2\): the mass-action law holds only in thermal equilibrium, and the light adds generation
\(n\) rises and \(p\) falls so that \(np\) stays equal to \(n_i^2\)
questions.explanation:
\(np = n_i^2\) came from \(G_{th} = knp\). With light, \(G = G_{th} + G_{opt}\) (Eq. 3.22), so the steady state has \(knp = G_{th} + G_{opt}\), giving \(np > n_i^2\).
Gotcha: light makes PAIRS, so \(n\) and \(p\) both rise; nothing pushes either down. This non-equilibrium situation is the basis of solar cells and of forward-biased diodes.

questions.prompt: Preview of why we dope silicon: pure Si at 300 K has \(\rho \approx 341\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}\) (with \(\mu_n + \mu_p = 1830\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\)). Heating to 350 K multiplies \(n_i\) by 22.1 (as computed from \(e^{-E_g/2kT}\)). Ignoring changes in mobility, what is the resistivity at 350 K, in kΩ·cm?
questions.explanation:
\(\sigma = q n_i(\mu_n+\mu_p)\) is proportional to \(n_i\), so \(\rho\) falls by the same factor:
\[\rho(350\ \mathrm{K}) = \frac{341}{22.1} \approx 15.4\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}\]
A resistor whose value drops by 20 times over a 50 K swing would be useless in a circuit (though fine as a temperature sensor). The next skill, doping, fixes the carrier concentration with impurities instead of leaving it to temperature.

questions.prompt: Preview of doping: suppose \(10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) extra free electrons are added to silicon by impurities (with no extra holes). After the sample returns to thermal equilibrium at 300 K, what is the hole concentration?
options: Still \(10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\); the impurities only add electrons
About \(10^{4}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\): extra electrons make holes recombine faster until \(np = n_i^2\) again
About \(10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), matching the electrons
Zero: every hole recombines
questions.explanation:
Mass action still holds in equilibrium: \(p = n_i^2/n = 10^{20}/10^{16} = 10^{4}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\).
The impurities raise \(n\) by a factor of \(10^6\), and recombination pushes \(p\) DOWN by the same factor. Holes become the rare 'minority' carriers. Holes don't vanish completely, because thermal generation keeps making a few.

questions.prompt: Preview of carrier concentration versus potential: a later skill shows that in equilibrium, a region with electron concentration \(n\) sits at an electrostatic potential \(\varphi = \frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{n}{n_i}\) relative to intrinsic silicon. Evaluate \(\varphi\) in mV for \(n = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), with \(kT/q = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\).
questions.explanation:
\[\varphi = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\times\ln(10^{6}) = 26 \times 13.82 \approx 359\ \mathrm{mV}\]
Handy shortcut: \(\ln 10 \times 26\ \mathrm{mV} \approx 60\ \mathrm{mV}\) per decade above \(n_i\), so 6 decades give about 360 mV. These potentials are what build the barrier inside a PN junction.
